planting.note: Set container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil; this tough Japanese species tolerates more sun and cold than many evergreen azaleas.

directions: Native to Japanese hillsides and open woodland, this semi-evergreen azalea bears masses of orange-red to salmon-pink flowers in late spring on a wiry, upright shrub. It is one of the hardiest and most sun-tolerant of the evergreen azalea species, a trait it has passed on to countless Kurume and Satsuki hybrids bred from it. Give it acidic, well-drained soil with consistent moisture and avoid heavy clay or alkaline sites. Light, renewal pruning right after bloom keeps older plants dense without sacrificing next year's flower buds.

planting.note: Grow outdoors year-round only in mild climates; elsewhere treat as a container or indoor-flowering shrub brought outside for summer and protected from freezing.

directions: This compact evergreen azalea from southern China and Taiwan is the principal wild parent behind the Belgian Indica and florist azaleas sold as potted winter-blooming houseplants worldwide. In its own right it is a dense, twiggy shrub smothered in funnel-shaped red, pink, or white flowers, often with darker blotching, in mid to late winter where climate allows. It needs acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and dislikes both drought and waterlogging. Where winters drop below the mid-teens it survives best in a sheltered courtyard or as a container specimen moved under cover for frost.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered woodland setting with deep, acidic, well-drained soil; mature specimens eventually form a small tree and need room to develop a trunk.

directions: A true tree-forming rhododendron from the Himalayan foothills, where it can reach forest-canopy heights and is Nepal's national flower. In cultivation it is usually seen as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with handsome, slightly curled dark green leaves and dense trusses of bell-shaped flowers, most often deep blood-red but also pink or white depending on provenance, opening in late winter to early spring. It is one of the most important wild parents behind large-flowered hardy hybrid rhododendrons bred in Britain and the Pacific Northwest. Give it shelter from hard freezes and drying wind, since both flower buds and new growth can be damaged well above the plant's ultimate cold tolerance.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil with morning sun; this deciduous azalea flowers before leafing out, so avoid sites with hard late frosts.

directions: A deciduous azalea native to Japanese mountain meadows and scrub, valued for brilliant orange-red to salmon flowers borne in rounded clusters on bare stems just before the leaves emerge in late spring. It is one of the principal ancestors of the fragrant, large-flowered Mollis azalea hybrids developed in European and American nurseries. The foliage often turns attractive shades of orange and red in autumn, giving two seasons of color from a single plant. It prefers cooler summer climates and resents hot, humid, poorly drained soil.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in a rock garden, container, or low border; its naturally dwarf, twiggy habit makes it a popular bonsai and edging subject.

directions: This naturally dwarf evergreen azalea grows wild on the volcanic slopes of Kyushu, Japan, forming low, dense mounds that are smothered in small purple, magenta, pink, or white flowers in late spring. It is a key parent of the compact Kurume azalea hybrids and is widely used by bonsai growers for its fine twiggy branching and small leaves. The low, tidy habit suits rock gardens, container culture, and the front of mixed shrub borders. Keep soil acidic and evenly moist, and shear lightly after flowering to maintain density.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil; exceptional cold hardiness makes this species valuable for northern gardens outside typical rhododendron range.

directions: Native to the mountains of the Caucasus along the Georgia-Turkey border, this evergreen species is distinguished by thick, dark green leaves with a dense white-to-fawn woolly coating on their undersides, giving the shrub a felted, silvery look from below. Rose-pink flowers open in trusses in late spring on a compact, rounded plant. Its outstanding winter hardiness has made it one of the most important parents in cold-climate rhododendron breeding programs in the northeastern United States. Site it with afternoon shade and wind protection in winter to prevent leaf scorch.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered woodland site with acidic, well-drained soil; late spring frosts can damage both flowers and tender new growth.

directions: Collected from the mountains of Yunnan and southeastern Tibet by plant hunter Frank Kingdon-Ward, this species bears wide, saucer-shaped, clear yellow flowers in loose trusses in mid to late spring on a rounded, medium-sized evergreen shrub. It is among the most important yellow-flowered wild rhododendrons used in breeding, lending its clean color and open flower form to many garden hybrids. It prefers a cool, humid woodland climate and performs poorly in hot, dry summers. Dappled shade and shelter from wind help preserve the smooth blue-green leaves.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in sun or partial shade; tolerates clipping into a dense formal hedge, screen, or large freestanding specimen.

directions: Native to the Iberian Peninsula, this broadleaf evergreen is one of the most widely planted large hedging and screening shrubs in mild temperate gardens, valued for glossy dark green leaves on striking wine-red new stems. Slender upright racemes of small, faintly almond-scented white flowers appear in late spring, followed by small dark purple cherries attractive to birds. It tolerates heavy clipping and urban pollution well, making it a dependable choice for formal hedges, topiary, and windbreaks. Give it reasonably fertile, well-drained soil and avoid waterlogged sites.

planting.note: Plant in fall to establish roots before dry summer heat; thrives in well-drained soil and needs little to no irrigation once established.

directions: This California chaparral native, sometimes called islay, forms a dense evergreen shrub or small tree with spiny, holly-like leaves distinct from the larger, smoother-leaved Catalina cherry of the Channel Islands. Short spikes of small white flowers appear in spring, followed by cherry-like fruit with a thin layer of sweet flesh over a large pit, historically gathered and processed by indigenous Californians. Extremely drought tolerant once established, it is a mainstay of low-water native hedges, screens, and wildlife plantings along the California coast and foothills. Avoid overhead watering and heavy soils, which encourage root rot in this summer-dry-adapted species.
